Any person found to have violated any of the provisions of these guideline shall be dealt with in accordance with the
provisions of the Teaching and Personnel Discipline and Student Discipline.
8.
General Statement on Obligations, Conflict of Interest, and Conflict of Commitment in the Intellectual Property Policy of the University of Cabuyao a.
General Obligations.
All individuals engaged in research, innovation, and intellectual property activities at the University of Cabuyao are obligated to adhere to ethical standards, transparency, and accountability.
This includes a commitment to honest and accurate reporting, responsible use of resources, and compliance with relevant laws and regulations governing intellectual property. b.
Conflict of Interest.
To maintain the integrity of the intellectual property process, individuals must disclose any potential or actual conflicts of interest that may compromise the unbiased and fair evaluation of IP matters.
Such conflicts could arise from personal, financial, or professional interests that may influence decision-making related to intellectual property ownership, protection, and commercialization. c.
Conflict of Commitment.
Individuals associated with the university must manage conflicts of commitment that may arise from simultaneous professional obligations outside the university.
Balancing external commitments with responsibilities to the University of Cabuyao is essential to ensure that intellectual property matters receive the necessary attention and dedication.
9.
Dispute Resolution.
In the event of disputes related to IP ownership, protection, or commercialization, the following dispute resolution process will be followed: a.

passages.title: UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.source: University LMS / UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.page_or_section: GUIDELINES > CHAPTER V INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS > Section 2. Specific Policies (pp. 105-106)
passages.text:
GUIDELINES > CHAPTER V INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS > Section 2. Specific Policies
Informal Resolution i.
Parties involved in the dispute are encouraged to engage in open communication and seek an informal resolution. ii.
Discussion may involve the relevant individuals, supervisors,
or department heads to address concerns and explore mutually agreeable solutions. b.
Mediation i.
If an informal resolution is not achieved, the parties may opt for mediation facilitated by a neutral third party. ii.
The mediator will work with the involved parties to explore options, clarify issues, and guide discussions toward a resolution. iii.
Mediation is voluntary, confidential, and aims to preserve relationships while addressing the core issues of the dispute. c.
Dispute Resolution Committee i.
If mediation does not result in a resolution, the matter may be referred to a Dispute Resolution Committee constituted by the University. ii.
The Committee will comprise individuals with expertise in relevant fields, including legal, academic, and administrative representatives. iii.
The Committee will conduct a thorough review of the dispute, consider relevant evidence, and provide recommendations for resolution. d.
Arbitration i.
In cases where resolution is not achieved through the Dispute Resolution Committee, parties may choose to engage in arbitration. ii.
Arbitration is a formal process where an impartial arbitrator or panel hears the case, reviews evidence, and issues a binding decision. iii.
The decision of the arbitrator is final and enforceable, providing a structured mechanism for resolving disputes.

e.
Legal Action i.
If all other avenues prove unsuccessful, parties retain the right to pursue legal action in accordance with applicable laws and regulations. ii.
Legal action should be considered as a last resort, and parties are encouraged to exhaust alternative dispute resolution mechanisms before pursuing litigation.

GUIDELINES > CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS > Section 2. Specific Policies
CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS PNC:PRE-GU-20 Section 1.
General Policies 1.
The University, through the Knowledge Management and Innovation Department, shall create a supportive environment for innovation and start-up projects, by providing necessary resources, facilities, and mentoring support to students and teaching and non-teaching personnel.
2.
The University shall encourage and incentivize students and teaching and non-teaching personnel to participate in innovation and start-up projects, by offering grants, seed funding, and other financial and non-financial support through partnership with government or private agencies.
3.
The University shall establish mechanisms to protect and commercialize intellectual property arising from innovation and start-up projects, by providing legal and technical support to students and teaching and non-teaching personnel.
4.
The University shall collaborate with industry partners and investors to facilitate the commercialization of innovation and start-up projects, by providing networking and matchmaking opportunities to students and faculty members.
5.
The University shall ensure that innovation and start-up projects are aligned with its philosophy and objectives, and that they adhere to ethical and legal standards Section 2.
Specific Policies 1.
Students, teaching, or non-teaching personnel who intend to venture into start-up projects shall submit the Innovation and Start-
up Project Form (PNC:PRE-FO-56) to KMID.
2.
It shall be evaluated by the Innovation Technical Committee using the Innovation and Start-Up Projects Evaluation Form (PNC:PRE-FO-58).
3.

passages.title: UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.source: University LMS / UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.page_or_section: GUIDELINES > CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS > Section 2. Specific Policies (p. 109)
passages.text:
GUIDELINES > CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS > Section 2. Specific Policies
KMID shall organized an Innovation Technical Committee (ITC) who shall guide the innovators-applicants.
It is a a group of experts who are responsible for reviewing and evaluating innovation-related projects and initiatives within an organization.
The committee is typically composed of three individuals with specialized knowledge and experience in innovation, technology, research and development, and related fields.
4.
Following are the roles of the ITC: a.
Evaluate new ideas and proposals: The committee reviews and evaluates new ideas and proposals submitted by individuals or teams within the organization.
They assess the feasibility, potential impact, and technical aspects of the proposals and provide recommendations for further development or implementation. b.
Develop innovation strategies: The committee works with the University to develop innovation strategies that align with the University's philosophy and objectives.
They identify areas of opportunity, potential risks, and help set priorities for innovation projects. c.
Provide technical expertise: The committee provides technical expertise and guidance to project teams, helping them to overcome technical challenges and identify solutions to complex problems. d.
Monitor progress: The committee monitors the progress of ongoing innovation projects, tracks key performance indicators, and provides feedback to project teams to ensure that they stay on track and achieve their goals.

passages.title: UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.source: University LMS / UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.page_or_section: GUIDELINES > CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS > Section 2. Specific Policies (p. 110)
passages.text:
GUIDELINES > CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS > Section 2. Specific Policies
e.
Foster a culture of innovation: The committee helps to foster a culture of innovation within the University by encouraging and supporting individuals and teams to think creatively and develop new ideas and solutions.
5.
Following are the processes to be observed. a.
Ideation i.
KMID shall create venues for ideation.
This involves generating and refining ideas for a new product, service, or technology.
The goal is to identify a gap in the market or a specific problem that needs to be solved. ii.
During the ideation process, it is important to identify and gather relevant knowledge about the problem or opportunity.
This can include both internal knowledge (such as knowledge about the organization and its processes) and external knowledge (such as knowledge about the market and industry trends). iii.
KMID shall organize a team who may help the innovators to ideate.
The team generates new ideas for innovative products, services, or business ventures.
This may involve brainstorming sessions, market research, and feedback from customers and stakeholders. b.
Screening and selection.
The KMID screens and evaluates the potential of the ideas based on criteria such as feasibility, market potential, and strategic fit.
The most promising ideas are selected for further development. c.
Concept development: The KMID and the team develop a concept for the product, service, or business venture, including features, benefits, and target markets. d.
Business planning.
The team develops a business plan for the start-up project, including financial projections, market analysis, and a marketing plan.

passages.title: UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.source: University LMS / UC-PnC Student Research and Innovation Manual
passages.page_or_section: GUIDELINES > CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS > Section 2. Specific Policies (p. 111)
passages.text:
GUIDELINES > CHAPTER VI MANAGEMENT OF INNOVATION AND START-UP PROJECTS > Section 2. Specific Policies
e.
Validation.
KMID shall assists the innovators to test and validate their ideas through research, market analysis, and customer feedback.
This helps to determine whether the idea is feasible, viable, and sustainable. f.
Resource allocation.
KMID assists in looking for resources, such as funding, personnel, and facilities, to support the development and launch of the start-up project. g.
Development.
Once the idea is validated, the project moves to the development stage.
This involves creating a prototype, building a minimum viable product (MVP), and refining the product or service based on user feedback. h.
Launch.
The launch stage involves bringing the product or service to market.
This may involve developing a marketing strategy, establishing distribution channels, and creating a launch plan i.
Growth.
After the product or service is launched, the focus shifts to growth and scaling.
This involves increasing market share, expanding into new markets, and attracting new customers. j.
Sustainability.
The final stage of the process involves ensuring the long-term sustainability of the start-up project.
This may involve developing a sustainable business model, establishing partnerships, and creating a strong brand identity.
